entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Royal Spanish Academy, established in 1713, stands as a cornerstone of the Spanish language and literature, headquartered in Madrid, Spain. Founded under the auspices of the Spanish monarchy, it was influenced by the Enlightenment ideals of order and rationality, aiming to standardize and preserve the Spanish language. Key figures in its inception included Juan Manuel Fernández Pacheco, the first director, and a group of intellectuals dedicated to promoting linguistic purity during a time when the Spanish Empire was expanding and facing linguistic diversification across its territories.

The Academy's primary mission was to create a comprehensive dictionary and grammar for the Spanish language, culminating in the publication of the first edition of the "Diccionario de la lengua española" in 1780. Over the centuries, it has published numerous works that define grammatical norms and enrich the Spanish lexicon, most notably the orthographic norms established in the "Ortografía" of 1741. The Academy also played a significant role in the promotion of Spanish literature, influencing writers like Miguel de Cervantes and Federico García Lorca, thereby shaping the canon of Spanish literature as we know it today.

As the custodian of the Spanish language, the Royal Spanish Academy significantly impacted various Spanish-speaking countries, ensuring linguistic cohesion across the Americas and Europe. Its authority has led to the establishment of similar institutions in other Spanish-speaking nations, fostering a sense of cultural identity tied to the language. The Academy's influence extends into modern times, adapting to the digital age while maintaining its commitment to the purity and evolution of Spanish.
